title: What Is a Contradiction? A Framing Piece
subtitle: How to distinguish a real contradiction from a difficult passage or textual variant.
summary: A serious comparison needs a fair test: identify two claims, ask whether their meanings really exclude each other, and examine the strongest contextual explanation. The Quran invites reflection on its coherence. Applying that invitation honestly strengthens an Islamic case; inflating differences or exempting Muslim claims from the same test does not.

seo.metaTitle: What Is a Contradiction? A Framing Piece | The Straight Path
seo.metaDescription: A contradiction occurs when two claims cannot both be true in the same sense, time, and respect.

sections.title: What Would Actually Count Against a Revelation?
sections.body:
If a text claims to convey the knowledge of an all-knowing God, a real contradiction matters. It would mean the competing claims cannot both be true in the same sense, at the same time, and about the same thing. A difference in detail is not enough.

The Islamic invitation is to apply that standard to the Quran as well as the Bible. Quran 4:82 makes reflection on the text part of the inquiry. This gives a seeker a concrete task, not a demand to dismiss difficulties on one side while celebrating them on the other.

sections.title: A Textbook Case: Who Incited David's Census?
sections.body:
In 2 Samuel 24, David orders a census treated as sinful. A plague follows. The chapter opens: "Again Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he moved David against them, saying, “Go, count Israel and Judah.”" (2 Samuel 24:1, World English Bible). In the later account, 1 Chronicles 21 opens: "Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to take a census of Israel." (1 Chronicles 21:1, World English Bible).

The Hebrew verb comes from *sut*, "to incite" or "entice." The WEB and KJV use "moved." NIV, ESV, and NASB use "incited." The verb is the same. The subject differs.

Samuel-Kings and Chronicles are separate works. Samuel-Kings reached near its present form during or after the sixth-century BC exile, using older sources. Chronicles is later, often dated to the fourth century BC, and retells history with different choices and theology. The census change is substantial: who incited David?

Gleason Archer treats it in *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties*. Sara Japhet discusses it critically. The case is genuine and long recognized across theological schools.

sections.title: Why the Coherence Challenge Matters
sections.body:
Quran 4:82 directs attention to the coherence of the proposed revelation. A message about God, human conduct, and judgment should not require its audience to affirm mutually exclusive claims without explanation. Its teachings must be read in context rather than reduced to isolated slogans.

The argument has limits. A consistent human document is possible; freedom from an identified contradiction does not by itself establish divine origin. The Quran's case also concerns its message, the credibility of its messenger, and the evidence of transmission. Coherence is a real test within that case, not a shortcut around the other questions.

A proposed explanation should therefore clarify the text and its circumstances. Calling every difficulty a mystery would make the test empty.

sections.title: Work Through One Example Fairly
sections.body:
Second Samuel 24:1 attributes the census impulse to the Lord, while 1 Chronicles 21:1 attributes it to Satan. The difference deserves explanation. A common Christian response distinguishes ultimate divine permission from Satan's immediate action. Other biblical texts use more than one level of agency, so that response is not merely a random invention.

Does it resolve the wording here? A seeker should ask whether the distinction fits the accounts and their wider context, and what assumptions it needs. Historical-critical readers may instead see a changed theological portrayal. Both assessments require reasons. Naming the two subjects alone does not settle which explanation is best.

This is how a useful objection becomes an argument: the claims, proposed resolution, and remaining difficulty are all visible.

sections.title: Three Judgments That Should Not Be Confused
sections.body:
1. **Possible:** an account can be imagined in which both statements are true. That may show a formal contradiction has not been proved.
2. **Plausible:** the proposed account fits the language, context, and ordinary evidence. This is a stronger judgment.
3. **Established:** there is positive evidence that the proposed account actually occurred. Possibility alone does not supply that evidence.

The same distinction applies when Muslims answer objections to the Quran. A plausible contextual reading is not automatically evasion, but a bare possibility should not be advertised as demonstrated history. Keeping the levels clear makes the discussion both firmer and fairer.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions About "Contradiction"
sections.body:
Lists of Bible or Quran contradictions often skip classification. They may count textual variants, harmonizable difficulties, interpretations, and logical contradictions together. That inflates rhetoric, not evidence.

Calling a problem harmonizable is not always an excuse. Some harmonies are weak. The census reading can draw on dual agency elsewhere: Job 1-2, 1 Kings 22, and Genesis 50:20. That is stronger than an ad hoc rescue, though it still needs judgment.

Quran 4:82 does not stop Muslim study of tension. Ibn Qutayba's hadith work and *mushkil al-Qur'an* literature show a long tradition of serious analysis.

Calling something interpretation is not evasion. Scholars debate every stable ancient text. Debate alone does not prove a defect.

sections.title: What This Contributes to the Islamic Case
sections.body:
A claim to revelation deserves confidence when it withstands serious examination rather than requiring special protection from it. Islam's invitation gains credibility when difficult passages are explained through their actual language and context, and weak attacks on other scriptures are willingly retired.

That standard does not decide every example in advance. It makes the next investigation meaningful. [Contradictions in the Bible](/articles/contradictions-in-the-bible) applies it to specific cases; [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) develops the positive reasons for accepting the Quran rather than assuming another text's difficulty proves Islam.

sections.title: Test an Example Before Accepting a List
sections.body: Choose one alleged contradiction and examine the full passages and the strongest response. A sound verdict is worth more than a long list of untested claims. The Islamic path asks for truthful inquiry that can lead to conviction, not victory through selective standards.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: What makes two claims contradictory?
A: They cannot both be true about the same thing, at the same time, and in the same respect. A difference in detail, scope, or viewpoint is not automatically a contradiction.

Q: Does a possible harmony settle what happened?
A: It may show that a contradiction is not logically inevitable. A plausible harmony also fits the language and context. Establishing that it actually happened requires positive evidence. Those are different judgments.

Q: Does coherence alone prove the Quran is revelation?
A: No. Quran 4:82 invites examination of coherence within the Quran's claim to revelation. A complete case also concerns its message, Muhammad's credentials, and transmission. A consistent human document is possible.

Q: Does every biblical difficulty defeat Christian belief?
A: No. A difficulty must be connected to the particular claim it challenges. Copying differences, literary purpose, and plausible context may matter. Christian accounts of inspiration should be assessed as their adherents actually hold them.

Q: How should a seeker begin?
A: Work through one example and its strongest response before accepting a long list. Apply the same standard to the Quran. [Contradictions in the Bible](/articles/contradictions-in-the-bible) gives specific cases, while [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) develops the positive revelation case.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties** — Gleason L. Archer. Evangelical harmonization reference.
- **I & II Chronicles: A Commentary** — Sara Japhet. Critical study of Chronicles.
- **Jesus, Interrupted** — Bart D. Ehrman. Historical-critical study of biblical differences.
- **Ta'wil Mukhtalif al-Hadith** — Ibn Qutayba. Classical study of difficult hadith reports.

quranVerses.translation: It is He who has sent down to you, [O Muhammad], the Book; in it are verses [that are] precise - they are the foundation of the Book - and others unspecific. As for those in whose hearts is deviation [from truth], they will follow that of it which is unspecific, seeking discord and seeking an interpretation [suitable to them]. And no one knows its [true] interpretation except Allah. But those firm in knowledge say, "We believe in it. All [of it] is from our Lord." And no one will be reminded except those of understanding.

bibleVerses.text: Again Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he moved David against them, saying, “Go, count Israel and Judah.”
Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to take a census of Israel.

Micaiah said, “Therefore hear Yahweh’s word. I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.
Yahweh said, ‘Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead?’ One said one thing; and another said another.
A spirit came out and stood before Yahweh, and said, ‘I will entice him.’
Yahweh said to him, ‘How?’
He said, ‘I will go out and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’
He said, ‘You will entice him, and will also prevail. Go out and do so.’
Now therefore, behold, Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; and Yahweh has spoken evil concerning you.”
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is today, to save many people alive.

furtherReading.title: Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties
furtherReading.author: Gleason L. Archer
furtherReading.note: A standard evangelical harmonization reference that illustrates the dual-causation approach to difficult biblical passages.

furtherReading.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)
furtherReading.author: Sara Japhet
furtherReading.note: A leading critical commentary examining how the Chronicler reworked material inherited from Samuel-Kings, including the census narrative's shift in the identity of the inciting agent.

furtherReading.title: Jesus, Interrupted: Revealing the Hidden Contradictions in the Bible
furtherReading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
furtherReading.note: A widely read presentation of the historical-critical approach to differences among biblical books.

furtherReading.title: Ta'wil Mukhtalif al-Hadith
furtherReading.author: Ibn Qutayba
furtherReading.note: A classical ninth-century work devoted to systematically resolving apparently conflicting hadith reports, illustrating the depth of the Islamic tradition's own internal tools for handling textual difficulty.
